front: 'Multiple alleles' is a population-level property. How many alleles at that locus does one diploid individual carry?
why: Two alleles per diploid individual is a supporting clarification, rarely scored

front: A 15:1 dihybrid ratio arises from {{c1::duplicate gene action}} — a dominant allele at EITHER locus produces the phenotype.
why: 15:1 duplicate gene action is a rare modified ratio not asked on the MCAT

front: A 9:3:4 dihybrid ratio indicates {{c1::recessive epistasis}} — the $aa$ genotype masks the second locus.
why: 9:3:4 recessive epistasis (Labrador) is the classic modified ratio commonly tested

front: A 9:7 dihybrid ratio signals {{c1::duplicate recessive (complementary gene) epistasis}} — homozygous recessive at either locus blocks the phenotype.
why: 9:7 complementary gene action is a secondary modified ratio

front: A dihybrid cross yields a 9:3:4 phenotypic ratio. What does the collapsed class indicate?
why: Near-restatement of the 9:3:4 recessive epistasis cloze card

front: A dihybrid testcross gives parentals at 42%+42% and recombinants at 8%+8%. Conclusion: the genes are {{c1::linked, 16 map units apart}}.
why: Converting testcross recombinant % to map units is a common calculation

front: A monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes gives a {{c1::3:1}} phenotypic ratio and a {{c2::1:2:1}} genotypic ratio.
why: Monohybrid 3:1 and 1:2:1 ratios are foundational, tested every year

front: A testcross of a dominant-phenotype plant yields 50 dominant : 50 recessive offspring. The tested parent is {{c1::heterozygous ($Aa$)}}.
why: Reading a 1:1 testcross as heterozygous is a common applied question

front: A testcross predicts 1:1:1:1 but yields 40:10:10:40. What does this show and what is the map distance?
why: Second worked linkage example; restates the 16-map-unit testcross card

front: A trait affecting almost only males, passed from unaffected carrier mothers to sons, is {{c1::X-linked recessive}}.
why: X-linked recessive pedigree recognition is tested every administration

front: A trait passed to all children of affected mothers and to none of an affected father's children is {{c1::mitochondrial}}.
why: Mitochondrial pedigree pattern is a core inheritance mode tested yearly

front: A trait present in every generation, in both sexes, with every affected child having an affected parent, is {{c1::autosomal dominant}}.
why: Autosomal dominant pedigree recognition is tested every administration

front: A trait that skips generations, affects both sexes equally, and clusters in consanguineous families is {{c1::autosomal recessive}}.
why: Autosomal recessive pedigree recognition is tested every administration

front: A trisomy 21 child has three distinct alleles at a chromosome 21 marker. Did nondisjunction occur in meiosis I or II?
why: Meiosis I vs II nondisjunction from allele count is a common passage reasoning step

front: A type O child is born to a type A mother and a type B father. What must the parents' genotypes be?
why: ABO parental genotype deduction is a perennial discrete

front: AB blood type is {{c1::codominance}} because both alleles produce detectable antigen, not a blend.
why: Near-restatement of the ABO codominance and dominance-types cards

front: An affected mother passes an X-linked recessive trait to ALL sons only if she is {{c1::homozygous affected}}; a carrier affects half her sons.
why: Son risk from carrier vs affected mother is a common X-linked probability

front: An obligate carrier in a dominant pedigree shows no phenotype yet has affected children. This is {{c1::incomplete penetrance}}.
why: Incomplete penetrance in a dominant pedigree is a standard twist

front: Cross $AaBb \times Aabb$: what is the probability of an $aabb$ offspring?
why: Product rule for mixed-locus crosses is used on essentially every exam

front: Crossing two yellow mice yields 2 yellow : 1 non-yellow instead of 3:1 because {{c1::the homozygous $A^Y A^Y$ genotype is embryonic lethal}}.
why: Recessive lethal 2:1 ratio is a commonly tested ratio distortion

front: Distinguish codominance from incomplete dominance at the phenotype level.
why: Restates the complete/incomplete/codominance card

front: Distinguish complete dominance, incomplete dominance, and codominance.
why: Complete/incomplete/codominance is a foundational every-year distinction

front: Distinguish incomplete penetrance from variable expressivity.
why: Penetrance vs expressivity is tested essentially every year

front: Distinguish nondisjunction, aneuploidy, and give an example.
why: Nondisjunction and aneuploidy examples are foundational, tested every year

front: Distinguish point mutations: silent, missense, nonsense.
why: Silent/missense/nonsense mutation types are tested every administration

front: Distinguish the sources of genetic variation in meiosis.
why: Sources of meiotic variation are commonly tested

front: For a monohybrid testcross of 100 offspring, a chi-square test uses {{c1::1}} degree of freedom.
why: Chi-square degrees of freedom is not tested on the MCAT biology section

front: For an autosomal recessive disease, the unaffected sibling of an affected child is a carrier with probability {{c1::2/3}}.
why: The 2/3 carrier conditional is a classic every-year trap

front: From $AaBb \times AaBb$, what fraction of offspring shows the dominant A phenotype but the recessive b phenotype?
why: Dihybrid 3/16 by product rule is a common application; the mixed-cross card is the anchor

front: How do you determine whether an organism with a dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous?
why: Restates the test cross definition/purpose card

front: How does a backcross differ from a testcross?
why: Backcross vs testcross is vocabulary with no tested reasoning content

front: How is autosomal recessive inheritance recognized in a pedigree?
why: Restates the autosomal recessive pedigree card with examples

front: How is X-linked recessive inheritance recognized?
why: Restates the X-linked recessive pedigree cards with examples

front: If 1 in 10,000 people has an autosomal recessive disease, what is the carrier frequency?
why: Carrier frequency from disease incidence is the core HW calculation

front: In a dihybrid cross $AaBb \times AaBb$, the fraction of offspring recessive for BOTH traits is {{c1::$1/16$}}.
why: Double recessive 1/16 is a common product-rule application

front: In a dihybrid testcross $AaBb \times aabb$, what offspring ratio shows the two genes assort independently?
why: 1:1:1:1 dihybrid testcross as the independent-assortment baseline is commonly needed

front: In ABO blood groups, $I^A$ and $I^B$ are {{c1::codominant}} with each other, while both are completely dominant over $i$.
why: ABO codominance plus dominance over i is a foundational every-year fact

front: In X-linked recessive pedigrees, an affected father transmits the trait to {{c1::no sons, but all daughters become carriers}}.
why: Affected father -> carrier daughters, unaffected sons is core X-linked logic

front: Man's brother has an AR disease; partner's carrier risk is 1/50. P(affected child) = {{c1::$2/3 \times 1/50 \times 1/4 = 1/300$}}.
why: Chained carrier-risk product problems are commonly tested

front: Marfan syndrome affects skeleton, lens, and aorta via one fibrillin-1 mutation. What inheritance concept does this illustrate?
why: Marfan is a secondary pleiotropy example; the definition card carries the content

front: One gene influencing many distinct phenotypes is {{c1::pleiotropy}} — e.g., the sickle allele causing anemia, splenomegaly, and malaria resistance.
why: Pleiotropy with the sickle example is commonly tested

front: Only 60 percent of people with a dominant allele show the trait, and those who do vary in severity.
why: Restates the penetrance vs expressivity card

front: Parents $I^A i \times I^B i$: which blood types can appear among their children?
why: IAi x IBi giving all four blood types is a common ABO question

front: Pattern baldness is dominant in males but recessive in females — a {{c1::sex-influenced}} trait, unlike sex-limited traits expressed in one sex only.
why: Sex-influenced vs sex-limited is secondary detail

front: Pedigree clue: an affected father has ALL affected daughters and NO affected sons. Mode = {{c1::X-linked dominant}}.
why: X-linked dominant father -> all daughters is a commonly tested pedigree clue

front: Pedigree clue: an affected mother transmits the trait to ALL her children, but an affected father transmits it to none. Mode?
why: Restates the mitochondrial inheritance cloze card

front: Pedigree clue: every affected individual has an affected parent and the trait appears in every generation. Mode?
why: Restates the autosomal dominant signature cloze card

front: Pedigree clue: the trait skips generations and appears in children of two unaffected parents. Mode = {{c1::autosomal recessive}}.
why: Restates the autosomal recessive signature cloze card

front: Red $\times$ white snapdragons give an all-pink $F_1$; the $F_2$ shows {{c1::1 red : 2 pink : 1 white}} — incomplete dominance.
why: Snapdragon 1:2:1 incomplete dominance is a standard example

front: Sickle cell allele behavior depends on the level of analysis. Explain the apparent contradiction.
why: Level-of-analysis dominance nuance is secondary

front: State Mendel's law of segregation and law of independent assortment.
why: Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment are foundational

front: State the Hardy-Weinberg equations and conditions.
why: Hardy-Weinberg equations and assumptions are tested every administration

front: The Bombay phenotype types as O despite $I^A$ or $I^B$ alleles because {{c1::homozygous $hh$ blocks H antigen synthesis}}.
why: Bombay phenotype is a secondary epistasis example

front: The maximum recombination frequency between two loci is {{c1::50 percent}}, which is indistinguishable from independent assortment.
why: RF cap at 50% equals independent assortment is a common conceptual question

front: The same chromosome 15 deletion causes Prader-Willi if paternal and Angelman if maternal. What explains this?
why: Prader-Willi/Angelman imprinting is the standard example but secondary

front: The single most decisive pedigree feature excluding X-linkage is {{c1::male-to-male transmission}}.
why: Male-to-male transmission excluding X-linkage is core pedigree logic

front: Two known carriers plan a child. What is P(child is a carrier GIVEN the child is unaffected)?
why: Restates the 2/3 conditional carrier probability card

front: Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis. What are the parents' genotypes and the recurrence risk?
why: Obligate carrier parents and independent 1/4 risk is a common counseling question

front: What is a frameshift mutation and why is it often severe?
why: Frameshift mutations are tested every administration

front: What is a test cross and what is its purpose?
why: Test cross definition and purpose is foundational, tested every year

front: What is genetic linkage and how does recombination frequency relate to distance?
why: Linkage and RF as map distance is core, used in calculations every year

front: What is pleiotropy vs. polygenic inheritance vs. epistasis?
why: Pleiotropy/polygenic/epistasis distinction is a perennial discrete

front: What is the expected phenotypic ratio of a monohybrid and a dihybrid cross (heterozygous parents)?
why: Monohybrid 3:1 and dihybrid 9:3:3:1 ratios are foundational

front: Why do some carrier females show mild Duchenne muscular dystrophy or hemophilia symptoms?
why: Manifesting carrier via skewed X-inactivation is second-tier detail

front: Why does a testcross use a homozygous recessive partner rather than a homozygous dominant one?
why: Why a testcross uses a recessive tester supports the test cross card

front: Why does consanguinity (e.g., first-cousin mating) specifically raise autosomal recessive disease risk?
why: Consanguinity raising recessive risk is a common reasoning question

front: Why has selection not eliminated the Huntington disease allele despite complete penetrance and lethality?
why: Huntington late onset and anticipation is secondary context
